name: Project 8

Status is recorded PHASE BY PHASE rather than as a single blob, per the brief's caution that early demonstrators must not be called 'active' in the mature-experiment sense: Phase I is `commissioning` (R&D demonstration), Phase II is `active` (physics-relevant CRES measurements on molecular tritium under way), Phase III is `proposed` (atomic-tritium source still in R&D). The record's top-level `status` reflects the most advanced confirmed phase (Phase II, active).

physics_goals.quote: our aim is to measure the absolute neutrino mass using tritium beta decays ... a new method of electron spectroscopy, Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy (CRES)
physics_goals.value: Measure the absolute neutrino mass via a high-precision, frequency-based tritium beta-decay spectrum measurement (Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy)

summary.plain: An experiment that measures the faint radio signal a single electron gives off when it spins in a magnetic field, aiming to weigh the neutrino. It began as a tabletop demonstration at the University of Washington and is now moving toward using real tritium gas.
summary.technical: Project 8: phased neutrino-mass programme using Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy (CRES) on tritium beta decay. Phase I (University of Washington, CRES first demonstrated in 2014) demonstrated single-electron CRES detection on 83mKr conversion electrons (15 eV resolution). Phase II achieved the first CRES measurement of the molecular-tritium beta spectrum. Phase III (CENPA-led atomic-tritium source R&D) targets the systematic limitations of molecular tritium, working toward a final design sensitivity of ~40 meV.

unique_capabilities.locator: Project 8 Phase II apparatus paper, abstract
unique_capabilities.quote: Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy (CRES) is a novel technique for the precise measurement of relativistic electron energy.
unique_capabilities.value: Frequency-based (not energy-based) single-electron spectroscopy, measuring the cyclotron radiation of individual beta-decay electrons in a magnetic field rather than their energy directly
